newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia plans to sell national rail company.
newsitem.headline: Australia plans to sell national rail company.

text.p: The Australian government said on Sunday it planned to sell its debt-laden Australian National (AN) rail business as part of a plan to revive the country's rail system and boost the economy by cutting transport costs.
"We are proposing to make AN for sale, make it available for sale," Transport Minister John Sharp said on television.
Sharp said it would cost the government about A$2 billion (US$1.62 billion) to prepare the business for sale.

"It's about a A$2 billion hole if you take everything into account that's needed to fix the problem," he said on Channel Nine's Sunday programme. He said AN would lose about A$250 million in the current financial year to June 30.

Sharp said there had already been expressions of interest to buy either all or part of AN, which operates mainly in South Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory and also runs the famous Indian-Pacific cross-continent passenger service.

Sharp said the government also hoped to sell its 40 percent stake in National Rail Corp (NRC), which operates interstate freight services. The other shareholders in NRC are the states of Victoria and New South Wales.
The government has said that Australian National, which has about 7,000 km (4,350 miles) of track, lost between A$135 million and A$148 million in the year to June 1996.
A consultant's report released earlier this year said AN had liabilities exceeding A$1 billion.
Part of this debt was accumulated financing assets that were transferred in 1993 to the NRC, an amalgam of more profitable federal and state rail operations, including some split from AN.
The result has been a collection of unprofitable operations in Australian National, which must also now compete with private rolling stock operators now allowed on the network.
Sharp said the government also planned to set up a publicly-owned track company to link all of Australia's capital cities on which privately owned trains would operate.
He said this would allow more participation by the private sector in the rail system to provide a competitive and reliable service that would ultimately cut transport costs.
Sharp said the government would assume all AN debts.
"There's about A$1 billion in actual debts," Sharp said.

"There's some A$400 odd million odd involved in tidying up the mess, and there's A$580 million worth of superannuation, which is unfunded, but which we'll have to pay, and there's also A$161 million which we're going to contribute building up our rail system on this inter-capital network which we propose to establish by July 1 of next year," he said.
The rationalisation of the rail network is vital to microeconomic reform, Sharp said. "It's one of the most significant microeconomic reforms ever undertaken in Australia."

"Reforming the rail system, such as we are proposing, will bring more dollars and cents to Australia than any other reform of the transport sector whether it be maritime, aviation or land," Sharp said.
He said the reforms would eventually bring more jobs, lower retail prices and improve the economy.
